analysis.one_liner: Cuts sugar price supports and import limits to bring sugar prices down for consumers and food makers.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 84 bipartisan cosponsors but never received a committee markup or a House vote before Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cut the government-guaranteed loan rates that prop up prices for sugarcane and sugar beet processors, make those processors repay any net cost the sugar program imposes on taxpayers, and phase out the program under which USDA buys surplus sugar from processors and resells it to ethanol producers. It would also repeal the marketing allotments that limit how much domestic processors can sell, and direct USDA to manage sugar import quotas to keep adequate supplies of sugar at reasonable prices.
analysis.who_benefits: American households and the food manufacturers that use sugar as a main ingredient. The bill lowers the government's price floor for sugar, ends USDA's purchases of surplus sugar, and directs USDA to manage import quotas to keep supplies adequate "at reasonable prices" — a shift aimed at pushing US sugar prices, which loan rates and import quotas have held well above world levels, downward. It also lets sugar-exporting countries transfer unused quota shares to others, so more import quota actually gets used.

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the loan rate the government guarantees for raw cane sugar in steps, from 18.75 cents per pound for the 2018 crop down to 18.00 cents by 2021, and sets the beet rate at 128.5% of the cane rate — a lower price floor than the program it replaces.
Requires USDA to recover any net cost of the sugar program from sugar processors, so taxpayers no longer absorb losses when the program runs in the red.

Extends the Feedstock Flexibility Program through 2019 and then terminates it — ending the arrangement under which USDA buys surplus sugar from domestic processors and resells it to ethanol producers.

Extends flexible marketing allotments through 2020 and then repeals them, ending the limits on how much sugar domestic processors may sell for domestic use, and directs USDA to administer the program to provide adequate supplies of sugar at reasonable prices.

Requires USDA to set tariff-rate quota imports to hit specific sugar stocks-to-use ratios (14.5% in 2019, 15% in 2020, 15.5% thereafter), a supply management rule designed to keep more sugar on the market, and allows countries to voluntarily transfer quota shares so unused import quota doesn't go to waste.

analysis.who_pays: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors, who would lose the high guaranteed loan rates, the government's surplus purchases, and the marketing allotments that shield their sales from competition. These losses would fall on a small number of growers concentrated in beet states like Minnesota and North Dakota and cane states like Florida and Louisiana, plus rural communities built around sugar processing. The bill's own Sense of Congress acknowledges the exposure by calling on the President to pursue elimination of all foreign government sugar subsidies before trade opens further.
analysis.who_pays_short: Sugar beet and cane growers and processors

drawbacks.text: Unilateral liberalization would expose US growers to foreign sugar produced with heavy government subsidies — a problem the bill itself flags by declaring it the sense of Congress that the President should seek the elimination of all direct and indirect foreign sugar subsidies and negotiate trade agreements that liberalize sugar trade globally.

The transition is real and concentrated: ending surplus purchases and marketing allotments and cutting loan rates over several crop years would cut revenue for sugar growers and processors and threaten jobs in sugar-dependent rural regions, even though the multi-year phase-down softens the blow.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains are broad but diffuse — lower ingredient costs for food manufacturers and modestly cheaper groceries for every household — while the costs are sharp and concentrated on roughly the growers and processors in a handful of states, who face subsidized foreign competition the bill can only ask the President to negotiate away. The multi-year phase-down and the no-net-cost recovery provision are honest attempts to soften both problems, and the trade-subsidy language shows supporters understood the fairness objection; on balance the bill trades a large consumer subsidy to a small industry for a managed transition, which is a defensible trade, though the growers' losses would be genuinely painful.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with broad bipartisan support in November 2017 and sent to the House Agriculture and Ways and Means Committees, neither of which ever took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Representative Virginia Foxx introduced the bill on November 7, 2017, with a bipartisan list of original cosponsors including both Republicans and Democrats.
It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and, in addition, to the Ways and Means Committee for the provisions under their jurisdiction.
The bill attracted 84 cosponsors, split 55 Republicans and 29 Democrats, but the action history shows no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote after the referral.
The 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019, and the bill expired without ever reaching the House floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors, who kept the price supports, surplus purchases, and import quota system that the bill would have phased out — the program's structure, and the above-market prices it supports, remained untouched.

for.name: Virginia Foxx
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to phase down sugar price supports, end USDA surplus sugar purchases, and repeal marketing allotments.

for.name: Danny K. Davis
for.role: U.S. Representative (D-IL), lead Democratic original cosponsor and Ways and Means member
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor, giving the bill Democratic support on the committee with jurisdiction over tariff provisions.

for.name: Coalition for Sugar Reform
for.role: Alliance of food manufacturers, sugar refiners, taxpayer and consumer groups
for.what_they_did: Publicly urged Congress to reform the sugar program and backed this legislation.

against.name: K. Michael Conaway
against.what_they_did: The Agriculture Committee, which he chaired, took no action on the bill — no hearing or markup — and it never left committee.

against.name: American Sugar Alliance
against.role: Trade association of US sugarcane and sugar beet growers and processors
against.what_they_did: Lobbied Congress to preserve the existing sugar program against reform efforts during this period.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan — 84 cosponsors split 55 Republicans and 29 Democrats — and the bill's failure in committee was regional rather than partisan, since sugar-program defenders in both parties sit on the Agriculture Committee.

industries.industry: Sugar beet and sugarcane growers and processors
industries.note: The bill cuts their guaranteed loan rates, ends USDA purchases of their surplus sugar, repeals the marketing allotments that restrict competitors' sales, and loosens import quotas — unwinding the structure that keeps US sugar prices well above world levels at consumer expense.

industries.industry: Sugar-using food manufacturers (candy, baked goods, cereals, beverages)
industries.note: Sugar is a top input cost, and the bill's mandate to keep supplies adequate at reasonable prices targets the import and allotment rules that inflate that cost; their gains track directly with cheaper food for consumers.

The bill requires stock levels adequate to meet the needs of the marketplace, 'including the efficient utilization of cane refining capacity,' and allows quota transfers between countries so refiners get a steadier supply of raw sugar.
Terminating the Feedstock Flexibility Program ends the flow of USDA-bought surplus sugar that the program resold to ethanol producers, removing a small subsidized feedstock source.
